questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose KU Leuven and Belgium as KU Leuven is recognised as one of the best universities in Europe. Moreover, I find Belgium interesting, both in its function as the 'heart of the EU' and also the cultural and political division between Flanders and Wallonia.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy as most information could be found on KU Leuven's website.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any assistance

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Rather easy, as I found and applied for KU Leuven residence halls through the university's website.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That Leuven is a small city and everything within the ring is relatively close to everything. Therefore there is no need to live “on campus”.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is really expensive to rent studios in Leuven - even as student accommodation, and in comparison to the cheap student accommodation in Copenhagen, living in Leuven is more expensive (but not more expensive than average prices in Copenhagen). I lived in a dorm room with a shared kitchen, toilets and bath facilities, with my hallway with 12 people. I payed 4500 DKK for that, and in comparison to this, in Copenhagen I am paying 3800 DKK to live in a little student studio with a bathroom and a tiny kitchen (but alone).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I remember it as fairly easy. I got an email explaining what to do in steps. The only thing to be cautious of was that one of the steps took 48 hours (if I remember correctly) and therefore it was advisable to begin the process a little time before arriving - a couple of days to a week in advance.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I do not know as I did not need any help.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Somewhat successful. I would have liked to register for a master’s course on voting behaviour, but even though the course was taught in English, I fulfilled the requirements about previous knowledge and level (as I am studying for my master’s), I was not allowed, because the course was only open to KU Leuven full-time students. As the professor teaching the course was recommended to me by a lector at UCPH, I found this very rigid and was disappointed that I was not allowed to register for the course.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Follow the instructions, and you should be fine.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Overall, the level of the courses was quite similar to the level on UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: For the most part, the style of teaching was rather similar: lecturing combined with active participation by students.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: “Labour Governance in Global Value Chains”; “Culture, Migration and Mobility”; “American Government and Politics”; “Keywords in Social and Cultural Anthropology”; “Human Computer Interaction”; “China and Global Politics”.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I could recommend the course “Labour Governance in Global Value Chains”. I found the theoretical frameworks presented interesting and useful in understanding the dynamics and complexity of global production networks and companies’ (non-/)compliance with human rights.

However, a course I would advise against registering for is “American Government and Politics”. Even though I did find the content interesting it did not make up for the lack of structure or the weird exam questions. There was no indication of which lectures would cover the which topics, and as a result, it was impossible to work out when you should have read the respective required readings. Furthermore, two out of four exam questions were incredibly specific and based on something that had only been briefly touched upon in a lecture, and were not covered in either the presentation slides or the required readings. One of the four questions was so clearly designed to ‘fish’ for a specific comment made during a lecture that it led to complaints from students; however, the professor’s response to this was that he had clearly stated that the exam would be based on ‘readings, presentations, and what has been said in class’ and that the exam questions were therefore entirely within the scope of the course. I thought the exam questions were very strange, and found them to stand in stark contrast to how I have experienced UCPH professors constructing exam questions. Normally these seek to assess how much knowledge a student has, rather than testing how well they have listened for a minor remark made during a given lecture. I felt the professor had an arrogant and unapproachable attitude and am disappointed with my experience of the course. I would therefore advise others against taking the course, at least whilst Professor Bart Kerremans is teaching it.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: No high, completely unexpected costs. However, I ended up spending much more money on food and social activities (drinks, pool, weektrips, etc.) than I anticipated.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Laundry detergent was for some reason much more expensive. Also, “ecological/bio” items were both more expensive and more inaccessible than in Denmark. Furthermore, the discount culture is a little different. Even though the overall price level might have been a bit lower in Leuven, I experienced that groceries were more expensive, as I usually buy discounted items in Denmark; however, in Belgium single items are rarely discounted. Instead, you can get the discount if you buy 2, 3, 4 or even higher numbers of an item. This was often not possible for me, because I did not need big amounts, as I only stayed in Belgium for one semester and furthermore did not have much space in the communal fridge or in my small pantry.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you paid for a sports card you gained access to a lot of sports facilities. If you paid for a culture card you could get a discount on many cultural things in Leuven and also had access to a few for free. Furthermore, student associations arranged all kinds of social activities, some for free, and some for a little amount of money to pay for costs of materials or transportation.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I would recommend participating in as many social activities during the orientation week as possible. It was a great way to meet other exchange students and to make friends.
In general social activities organised by the student associations is great fun and a good way to meet new people throughout the whole semester.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Other cities in Belgium or in neighbouring countries. For example, Paris and Amsterdam are quite close (and actually even cheaper to visit by Flixbus or BlaBla car than by train)

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy, as Flemish culture in many ways resembles Danish. Of course there are some differences, but overall it was not difficult to adjust to local culture.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Being open, warm and friendly is the best you can do. Also, Belgians are much more talkative towards internationals when out drinking, and therefore these are also good opportunities to get to know them. In everyday life, they are often keeping more to themselves; in this way they are actually quite like Danish people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: One of the things I appreciated most about Belgian culture was their ability to enjoy sunny weather and to always find an opportunity to have a cosy time over a beer with friends.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Begin the process with the pre-approval and the learning agreement very early on, as there might be a lot of obstacles along the way.
2) Participate in as much of the orientation programme as possible - it is a terrific way to meet other international students and to make friends.
3) Do not plan a lot of visits from home (especially towards the end) - a few visits are nice, but they might also limit opportunities to do things with your new friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Maybe that the canteen food (Alma) is quite boring most of the time . Instead I would recommend going to places such as Thai House (5 euros for a meal. I recommend pad thai and the red curry) and Pain Louvain (sandwich place. I recommend the chicken BLT (5,5 euros)).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know and becoming friends with people of other nationalities. Also becoming even more secure speaking English.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Getting in contact with the responsible people for the learning agreement and pre-approval at UCPH. It was very difficult to get my learning agreement signed by all parties before the deadline. It was signed after the deadline, which was a very difficult and stressful experience, especially considering I was in Belgium. I felt very alone and powerless in this, and it would have been nice if one specific person had been in charge of making sure everything worked out. Instead, I was left to write more and more desperate emails and call phones that would almost never be picked up. I hope that this was an isolated case due to a particularly busy period, but for me, this was the greatest challenge of the exchange, as I was really scared I would be unenrolled from my host university due to missed final deadlines set by the host univeristy.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
